newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Dyno explosives profit up but chemicals off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dyno explosives profit up but chemicals off.

text.p: Norway's Dyno Industrier ASA said on Friday its explosives business improved profitability in the first nine months of 1996 while chemicals continued to suffer from a weaker market for methanol.
For the year, the company said further gains in explosives were unlikely to offset lower chemicals' earnings.

"Results for 1996 as a whole will be significantly affected by the much lower methanol prices achieved this year compared to 1995. This will only to a certain extent be compensated by increased earnings from explosives operations," a company statement said.
Dyno posted pre-tax profits of 275 million crowns in the period to September 30 compared with 486 million crowns a year ago. The 1995 figure included an extraordinary gain of 93 million crowns.
Nine-month operating profit amounted to 342 million crowns versus 538 million crowns.
The operating profit for explosives doubled to 179 million crowns against 89 million crowns, while that for chemicals slumped to 162 million crowns from 424 million crowns.

Dyno attributed more than 50 percent of the decline in chemicals to the fall in methanol prices, while reduced raw materials prices for other chemicals divisions resulted in lower sales prices for finished goods.

"While explosives overall improved its position, results for chemicals as a whole were affected by a weaker European market and considerably lower earnings from the corporation's methanol production than in the same period in 1995," the company said.
In the third quarter, explosives recorded an operating profit of 73 million crowns versus a loss of 35 million crowns in the corresponding 1995 quarter.

"Measures implemented to improve efficiency and positive developments in all markets have led to a clear improvement in profitability for all three explosives divisions during the third quarter compared to the year before."

The operating profit for plastics rose a moderate seven percent to 59 million crowns, while the particles division swung into the black to book an operating result of five million crowns compared with a loss of five million crowns a year ago.
Dyno said it expected a cyclical improvement in the European economy towards the end of 1996 and on into 1997.
"This will probably lead to a higher level of activity in the wood processing industry next year," it said.

It forecast growth in the Australian mining industry and economic growth in southeast Asia to continue. In North America the construction industry would likely maintain current levels while demand for explosives would show moderate growth, Dyno said.
